source.title: Chebyshev Sets, Klee Sets, and Chebyshev Centers with respect to Bregman Distances: Recent Results and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: Let X = R^n, let f: X -> [-∞,+∞] be a Legendre function, let U = int dom f, let C be a nonempty closed subset of U, and let D(x,y) = f(x) - f(y) - <∇f(y), x-y> denote the Bregman distance. A set C is left D-Chebyshev when, for every y in U, the left nearest-point map P_C^left(y) = {x in C | D(x,y) = inf_{z in C} D(z,y)} is a singleton. Fact 3.1 states that if f is supercoercive and C is left D-Chebyshev, then C is convex. Is the supercoercivity assumption in that result actually necessary?
accepted.context_brief: Supercoercivity in left Bregman Chebyshev convexity

evidence.quote: Definition 1.7 (Chebyshev sets) The set C is a left Chebyshev set with respect to the Bregman distance, or simply ←−D-Chebyshev, if for every y ∈ U, ←−PC(y) is a singleton.
Fact 3.1 (←−D-Chebyshev sets) (See [7, Theorem 4.7].) Suppose that f is supercoercive and that C is ←−D-Chebyshev. Then C is convex.
Problem 1. Is the assumption that f be supercoercive in Fact 3.1 really essential?

accepted.question_text: Let X = R^n, let f be a Legendre function with U = int dom f and conjugate f*, and let C be a nonempty closed subset of U. Write C* = ∇f(C) and U* = int dom f*. A set C is right D-Chebyshev when, for every x in U, the right nearest-point map P_C^right(x) = {y in C | D(x,y) = inf_{z in C} D(x,z)} is a singleton. Fact 3.2 states that if dom f = X, C* is contained in U*, and C is right D-Chebyshev, then C* is convex. Are the assumptions dom f = X and C* ⊆ U* actually necessary for that conclusion?
accepted.context_brief: Hypotheses in right Bregman Chebyshev convexity

evidence.quote: Similarly, the set C is a right Chebyshev set with respect to the Bregman distance, or simply −→D-Chebyshev, if for every x ∈ U, −→PC(x) is a singleton.
Fact 3.2 (−→D-Chebyshev sets) (See [7, Theorem 7.3].) Suppose that dom f = X, that C∗ ⊆ U∗, and that C is −→D-Chebyshev. Then C∗ is convex.
Problem 2. Are the assumptions that f have full domain and that C∗ ⊆ U∗ in Fact 3.2 really essential?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a Legendre function f on X = R^n with full domain dom f = X such that f is not quadratic, yet every nonempty closed convex subset C of X is right D-Chebyshev with respect to the Bregman distance D induced by f? Equivalently, is there a nonquadratic full-domain Legendre function for which every closed convex C has a unique right Bregman nearest point from each x in X? The paper notes that if such an f exists, then its gradient map ∇f would be nonaffine and would preserve convexity.
accepted.context_brief: Nonquadratic full-domain Legendre functions with universal right Chebyshev property

evidence.quote: Similarly, the set C is a right Chebyshev set with respect to the Bregman distance, or simply −→D-Chebyshev, if for every x ∈ U, −→PC(x) is a singleton.

Fact 3.4 raises two intriguing questions. Apart from the case of quadratic functions, are there instances of f where f has full domain and where every closed convex subset of U is −→D-Chebyshev? Because of Fact 3.2, an affirmative answer to this question would imply that ∇ f is a (quite surprising) nonaffine yet convexity-preserving transformation.

Problem 3. Does there exist a Legendre function f with full domain such that f is not quadratic yet every nonempty closed convex subset of X is −→D-Chebyshev? In view of Fact 3.1, the gradient operator ∇ f of such a function would be nonaffine and it would preserve convexity.

accepted.question_text: Let f be the negative-entropy Legendre function from Example 1.1(ii), whose domain interior is the strictly positive orthant R^n_{++}. For the Bregman distance induced by this f, characterize exactly which subsets C of the strictly positive orthant are right D-Chebyshev; that is, determine precisely for which sets C every x in R^n_{++} has a unique right Bregman nearest point in C. The source notes that this class contains all closed convex subsets and also some nonconvex subsets.
accepted.context_brief: Right Bregman Chebyshev sets for negative entropy

evidence.quote: (ii) negative entropy: f(x) = ( ∑j xj ln(xj) − xj, if x ≥ 0; +∞, otherwise. Note that U = Rn ++ in (ii) and (iii).

Combining Example 3.3 and Fact 3.4, we deduce that — when working with the negative entropy — if C is convex, then C is −→D-Chebyshev but not vice versa. Is it possible to describe the −→D-Chebyshev sets in this setting?

Problem 4. Is it possible to characterize the class of −→D-Chebyshev subsets of the strictly positive orthant when f is the negative entropy? Fact 3.4 and Example 3.3 imply that this class contains not only all closed convex but also some nonconvex subsets.

accepted.question_text: Assume f is a Legendre function on X = R^n that is twice continuously differentiable on U = int dom f and has positive-definite Hessian ∇^2 f(y) for every y in U. Fact 3.5 states that if, in addition, f is supercoercive, then the left Bregman nearest-point map P_C^left is almost everywhere and generically single-valued on U. Is the supercoercivity assumption actually necessary for this almost-everywhere and generic single-valuedness conclusion?
accepted.context_brief: Supercoercivity in a.e. single-valued left nearest map

evidence.quote: Fact 3.5 (See [7, Corollary 5.6].) Suppose that f is supercoercive, that f is twice continuously differentiable, and that for every y ∈ U, ∇2 f(y) is positive definite. Then ←−PC is almost everywhere and generically single-valued on U.
It would be interesting to see whether or not supercoercivity is essential in Fact 3.5.
Problem 5. Is the assumption that f be supercoercive in Fact 3.5 really essential?

accepted.question_text: Assume f is a Legendre function on X = R^n that is twice continuously differentiable on U = int dom f, has positive-definite Hessian ∇^2 f(y) for every y in U, and let C be bounded. Fact 4.4 states that if f is also supercoercive, then the left Bregman farthest-point map Q_C^left is almost everywhere and generically single-valued on U. Is the supercoercivity assumption actually necessary for this almost-everywhere and generic single-valuedness result?
accepted.context_brief: Supercoercivity in a.e. single-valued left farthest map

evidence.quote: Fact 4.4 (See [7, Corollary 5.2.(ii)].) Suppose that f is supercoercive, that f is twice continuously differentiable, that for every y ∈ U, ∇2 f(y) is positive definite, and that C is bounded. Then ←−QC is almost everywhere and generically single-valued on U.
Again, it would be interesting to see whether or not supercoercivity is essential in Fact 4.4.
Problem 6. Is the assumption that f be supercoercive in Fact 4.4 really essential?

accepted.question_text: Section 7 defines, in the Euclidean setting, λ-Chebyshev functions as lower-semicontinuous proper functions g for which the proximal map P_λ g(x) = argmin_w ( g(w) + (1/(2λ))||x-w||^2 ) is single-valued on X, μ-Klee functions as functions g for which the farthest map Q_μ g(y) = argmax_x ( (1/(2μ))||y-x||^2 - g(x) ) is single-valued on X, and the μ-Chebyshev point p_μ as the unique element of argmin φ_μ g when that minimizer set is a singleton. When the halved Euclidean distance in these constructions is replaced by Bregman distances induced by a Legendre function, what are the correct characterizations of the resulting Chebyshev-function, Klee-function, and Chebyshev-point notions?
accepted.context_brief: Function-based Bregman analogues of Chebyshev and Klee theory

evidence.quote: Definition 7.4 (i) We say that g is λ-Chebyshev if Pλg is single-valued on X. (ii) We say that g is µ-Klee if Qµg is single-valued on X.

Definition 7.9 (Chebyshev points) The set of µ-Chebyshev points of g is argmin φµg. If argmin φµg is a singleton, then we denote its unique element by pµ and we refer to pµ as the µ-Chebyshev point of g.
Problem 7. For the Chebyshev functions and Klee functions, we have used the halved Euclidean distance. What are characterizations of f and Chebyshev point of f when one uses the Bregman distances?

accepted.question_text: Section 7 develops Euclidean-space results for λ-Chebyshev functions, μ-Klee functions, and μ-Chebyshev points of lower-semicontinuous proper functions on X = R^n. How do those function-based results extend from finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces to Hilbert spaces, or even to general Banach spaces?
accepted.context_brief: Extending function-based Chebyshev/Klee theory beyond Euclidean space

evidence.quote: Chebyshev set and Klee set problems can be generalized to problems involving functions. Throughout this section, (54) g : X → [−∞, +∞] is lower semicontinuous and proper.
Problem 8. How do the results on Chebyshev functions and Klee functions extend to Hilbert spaces or even general Banach spaces?
